```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(metafor)
library(patchwork)

# one palette for the whole deck
pal <- c(navy = "#12355B", rust = "#C8553D", teal = "#1F6F8B",
         sand = "#E9C46A", grey = "#6B7785", soft = "#EEF3F7")

theme_ylnc <- function(base_size = 16) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = pal[["navy"]]),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = pal[["grey"]]),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = pal[["grey"]]),
      legend.position = "top"
    )
}
theme_set(theme_ylnc())

# ---- Example data: BCG vaccine trials (Colditz et al. 1994; ships with metafor) ----
bcg <- dat.bcg |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(study = str_glue("{author} ({year})") |> as.character())

# effect sizes: log risk ratio and its sampling variance, per study
bcg_es <- bcg |>
  mutate(
    # log RR = log( (a/(a+b)) / (c/(c+d)) )
    yi  = log((tpos / (tpos + tneg)) / (cpos / (cpos + cneg))),
    vi  = 1 / tpos - 1 / (tpos + tneg) + 1 / cpos - 1 / (cpos + cneg),
    sei = sqrt(vi),
    lo  = yi - 1.96 * sei,
    hi  = yi + 1.96 * sei
  )

fe <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "FE")
re <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "REML")
re_dl <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "DL")
re_hk <- rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "REML", test = "knha")
re_pred <- predict(re, transf = exp)

fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
```

# Why meta-analysis? {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## What is a meta-analysis?

- A **reproducible** method to answer a research question by collecting **all** available studies on it
- Uses **statistical techniques** to combine the results of individual studies
- Draws **new conclusions** from the pooled data

::: {.keybox}
**Systematic review** = the whole process (question, search, appraisal, synthesis).<br>
**Meta-analysis** = the optional *statistical* step inside it.
:::

::: {.small .muted}
Every meta-analysis should sit inside a systematic review. Not every systematic review needs a meta-analysis.
:::

## Why combine studies?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Precision:** many small trials, each underpowered, together give a narrow CI
- **Consistency:** does the effect hold across settings, populations, doses?
- **Conflict resolution:** "positive" and "negative" trials can agree once pooled
- **New questions:** explore *why* results differ (subgroups, meta-regression)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| label: figx-precision
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
set.seed(42)
tibble(k = 1:12) |>
  mutate(
    n_cum = cumsum(rep(120, 12)),
    se    = sqrt(4 / n_cum)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, 1.96 * se)) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["teal"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["teal"]], size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of similar studies pooled",
    y = "Half-width of 95% CI",
    title = "More studies, narrower interval",
    subtitle = "Each study n = 120"
  )
```
:::
::::

## When **not** to meta-analyse

- Studies answer **different questions** (apples and oranges)
- Outcomes are measured in ways that **can't be put on one scale**
- Studies are at **high risk of bias** (garbage in, garbage out)
- **Very large, unexplained heterogeneity**: a single number would mislead
- **Selective reporting** has removed much of the evidence

::: {.keybox}
A precise pooled estimate of **biased** studies is a precisely wrong answer.
Narrative or structured synthesis (e.g. SWiM) is a legitimate alternative.
:::

# The workflow {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## From question to pooled estimate

```{r}
#| label: figx-workflow
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.6
steps <- tibble(
  step = c("Question\n(PICO)", "Write\nprotocol", "Search", "Screen &\nselect",
           "Extract\ndata", "Risk of\nbias", "Meta-\nanalysis", "Certainty\n(GRADE)"),
  x = seq_along(step),
  stat = x == 7
)

steps |>
  ggplot(aes(x, 1)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x + 0.42, xend = x + 0.58, y = 1, yend = 1),
               data = filter(steps, x < max(x)),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"),
               colour = pal[["grey"]]) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = stat), width = 0.86, height = 0.8, colour = NA) +
  geom_text(aes(label = step, colour = stat), size = 5.2, lineheight = 0.9, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pal[["soft"]], `TRUE` = pal[["rust"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pal[["navy"]], `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 8.5), ylim = c(0.5, 1.5)) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.small}
- Register the protocol (PROSPERO) **before** you see the results
- Report with **PRISMA 2020**: flow diagram, checklist, and the full search strategy
:::

## Collecting data: what to abstract

| Category | Columns |
|---|---|
| Study info | Study ID, author, year, country, design |
| Population | Description, age (mean/range), sex (%) |
| Sample size | n intervention, n control |
| Intervention | Name & dose, comparator, follow-up |
| Outcome data | Events/totals, or mean & SD per arm |
| Effect estimates | Effect size, 95% CI, p-value |
| Quality | Risk of bias, conflicts of interest, funding |

::: {.small .muted}
Pilot the form on 2–3 studies, extract in **duplicate**, and write to investigators for missing data.
:::

## Keep the data tidy

One row per study, one column per variable. This is what our BCG data look like:

```{r}
#| label: tblx-bcg
bcg |>
  select(study, tpos, tneg, cpos, cneg, ablat, alloc) |>
  slice_head(n = 7) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Study", "TB (vacc.)", "No TB (vacc.)", "TB (ctrl)", "No TB (ctrl)",
                  "Latitude", "Allocation"),
    align = "lrrrrrl"
  )
```

::: {.small .muted}
… 13 trials in all. `dat.bcg` ships with the **metafor** package (Colditz et al., *JAMA* 1994).
:::

## Risk of bias comes before pooling

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Within studies (RoB 2 / ROBINS-I)**

- Randomisation & allocation concealment
- Deviations from intended intervention
- Missing outcome data
- Measurement of the outcome
- Selective reporting
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Across studies (reporting biases)**

- Publication bias
- Time-lag bias
- Language bias
- Citation bias
- Duplicate publication
- Location bias
:::
::::

::: {.keybox}
Use RoB judgements in the analysis: sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk studies, or subgroup by RoB.
:::

# Effect measures {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## Choosing an effect measure

| Outcome type | Common measures | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dichotomous | **Risk ratio**, odds ratio, risk difference | TB yes/no |
| Continuous, same scale | **Mean difference (MD)** | SBP in mmHg |
| Continuous, different scales | **Standardised MD** (Hedges' *g*) | Depression scores |
| Time to event | **Hazard ratio** | Survival |
| Counts & rates | Rate ratio | Falls per person-year |

::: {.small}
Ratio measures are pooled on the **log scale** and back-transformed for presentation.
:::

## Computing a study's effect: the 2 × 2 table

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
|  | Event | No event |
|---|---|---|
| **Vaccine** | *a* | *b* |
| **Control** | *c* | *d* |

$$
\text{RR} = \frac{a/(a+b)}{c/(c+d)}
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\ln \text{RR}) = \tfrac{1}{a} - \tfrac{1}{a+b} + \tfrac{1}{c} - \tfrac{1}{c+d}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| label: code-es
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
bcg_es <- bcg |>
  mutate(
    yi  = log((tpos / (tpos + tneg)) /
              (cpos / (cpos + cneg))),
    vi  = 1/tpos - 1/(tpos + tneg) +
          1/cpos - 1/(cpos + cneg),
    sei = sqrt(vi)
  )

# or let metafor do it:
escalc(measure = "RR",
       ai = tpos, bi = tneg,
       ci = cpos, di = cneg,
       data = bcg)
```
:::
::::

# Pooling: fixed vs random effects {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## Meta-analysis is a two-stage process

1. **Stage 1:** compute an effect estimate $y_i$ and its variance $v_i$ for **each study**
2. **Stage 2:** combine them as a **weighted average**

$$
\hat\theta = \frac{\sum_i w_i \, y_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad w_i = \frac{1}{v_i}
\qquad \text{SE}(\hat\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\sum_i w_i}}
$$

::: {.keybox}
**Inverse-variance weighting:** precise (usually larger) studies count for more.
It is *not* a simple average and *not* pooling of raw patients.
:::

## Inverse-variance pooling by hand, the tidy way

```{r}
#| label: code-iv
#| echo: true
pooled_fe <- bcg_es |>
  mutate(wi = 1 / vi) |>
  summarise(
    theta = sum(wi * yi) / sum(wi),
    se    = sqrt(1 / sum(wi))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    RR    = exp(theta),
    lower = exp(theta - 1.96 * se),
    upper = exp(theta + 1.96 * se)
  )
pooled_fe
```

::: {.small .muted}
Identical to `rma(yi, vi, data = bcg_es, method = "FE")`: pooled RR = `r fmt(exp(coef(fe)))` (95% CI `r fmt(exp(fe$ci.lb))` to `r fmt(exp(fe$ci.ub))`).
:::

## Two models, two different questions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Fixed (common) effect**

- One true effect $\theta$ shared by all studies
- Differences between studies = **sampling error only**
- Answers: *"What is the best estimate of this common effect?"*
- Methods: inverse variance, Mantel–Haenszel, Peto
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Random effects**

- True effects **vary** across studies: $\theta_i \sim N(\mu, \tau^2)$
- Two sources of variation: within ($v_i$) + between ($\tau^2$)
- Answers: *"What is the **average** effect, and how much does it vary?"*
- Weights: $w_i^* = 1 / (v_i + \tau^2)$
:::
::::

::: {.keybox .small}
Choose the model on **conceptual** grounds in your protocol, not after peeking at *I*².
:::

## Random effects spreads the weight

```{r}
#| label: figx-weights
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.2
wts <- bcg_es |>
  mutate(
    `Fixed effect`   = weights(fe),
    `Random effects` = weights(re)
  ) |>
  select(study, `Fixed effect`, `Random effects`) |>
  pivot_longer(-study, names_to = "model", values_to = "weight") |>
  mutate(study = fct_reorder(study, weight, .fun = max))

wts |>
  ggplot(aes(weight, study, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(pal[["grey"]], pal[["rust"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Weight in pooled estimate", y = NULL,
       title = "Large trials dominate under fixed effect",
       subtitle = str_glue("τ² = {fmt(re$tau2)}: smaller trials get a bigger say under random effects"))
```

## Estimating the between-study variance τ²

| Estimator | Notes |
|---|---|
| DerSimonian–Laird (DL) | Classic, simple; underestimates τ² when *k* is small |
| **REML** | Recommended default in most software today |
| Paule–Mandel | Good alternative, also recommended |

**Hartung–Knapp (HKSJ) adjustment** widens the CI to reflect uncertainty in τ², especially with few studies.

```{r}
#| label: tblx-estimators
list(`DL` = re_dl, `REML` = re, `REML + HKSJ` = re_hk) |>
  imap(\(m, nm) tibble(
    Method = nm,
    `Pooled RR` = fmt(exp(m$b[1])),
    `95% CI` = str_glue("{fmt(exp(m$ci.lb))} to {fmt(exp(m$ci.ub))}"),
    `τ²` = fmt(m$tau2, 3)
  )) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lccc")
```

# Heterogeneity {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## Is the variation more than chance?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Visual:** do the CIs overlap?
- **Cochran's Q:** $Q = \sum w_i (y_i - \hat\theta)^2$, tests $H_0$: all studies share one effect. Low power with few studies.
- ***I*²** $= \frac{Q - df}{Q}$: % of variability due to real differences, not chance
- **τ²:** the *size* of the between-study variance, on the effect scale
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
| *I*² | Rough guide (Cochrane) |
|---|---|
| 0–40% | might not be important |
| 30–60% | moderate |
| 50–90% | substantial |
| 75–100% | considerable |

::: {.small}
BCG: Q = `r fmt(re$QE, 1)` (df = `r re$k - 1`), *I*² = `r fmt(re$I2, 0)`%, τ² = `r fmt(re$tau2)`
:::
:::
::::

## Same pooled effect, very different stories

```{r}
#| label: figx-hetero
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.2
set.seed(2025)
sim_studies <- function(tau, label, k = 8) {
  tibble(
    study = str_c("Study ", 1:k),
    sei   = runif(k, 0.12, 0.25),
    yi    = rnorm(k, -0.4, tau) + rnorm(k, 0, sei),
    scenario = label
  )
}

sims <- bind_rows(
  sim_studies(0.02, "Low heterogeneity"),
  sim_studies(0.45, "High heterogeneity")
) |>
  mutate(scenario = fct_inorder(scenario))

i2_lab <- sims |>
  nest(.by = scenario) |>
  mutate(
    fit   = map(data, \(d) rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d)),
    label = map_chr(fit, \(f) str_glue("I² = {fmt(f$I2, 0)}%"))
  ) |>
  select(scenario, label)

sims |>
  ggplot(aes(exp(yi), fct_rev(study))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = pal[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(-0.4), colour = pal[["rust"]], alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = exp(yi - 1.96 * sei), xmax = exp(yi + 1.96 * sei)),
                 height = 0, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(size = 1 / sei^2), shape = 15, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_text(data = i2_lab, aes(x = 2.6, y = 8.4, label = label),
            hjust = 1, size = 5.5, colour = pal[["rust"]], fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 5), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~scenario) +
  labs(x = "Risk ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16))
```

## Prediction interval: where the *next* study may land

- The CI tells us about the **average** effect
- The **95% prediction interval** tells us the range of true effects in a **new setting**

::: {.keybox}
BCG pooled RR = **`r fmt(re_pred$pred)`** (95% CI `r fmt(re_pred$ci.lb)` to `r fmt(re_pred$ci.ub)`)<br>
95% prediction interval: **`r fmt(re_pred$pi.lb)` to `r fmt(re_pred$pi.ub)`**
:::

On average BCG protects, but in some settings it may do little or nothing.
Report the prediction interval whenever you fit a random-effects model.

# Reading a forest plot {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## The BCG forest plot

```{r}
#| label: figx-forest
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6.2
forest_df <- bcg_es |>
  mutate(
    weight = weights(re),
    label  = str_glue("{fmt(exp(yi))} [{fmt(exp(lo))}, {fmt(exp(hi))}]"),
    wlab   = str_glue("{fmt(weight, 1)}%")
  ) |>
  arrange(year) |>
  mutate(row = rev(seq_len(n())) + 1)

diamond <- tibble(
  x = exp(c(re$ci.lb, re$b[1], re$ci.ub, re$b[1])),
  y = c(0, 0.35, 0, -0.35)
)
pool_lab <- str_glue("{fmt(exp(re$b[1]))} [{fmt(exp(re$ci.lb))}, {fmt(exp(re$ci.ub))}]")

forest_df |>
  ggplot(aes(y = row)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = pal[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(re$b[1]), colour = pal[["rust"]], linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = exp(re_pred$pi.lb |> log()), xend = exp(re_pred$pi.ub |> log()),
                   y = -0.9, yend = -0.9), colour = pal[["rust"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = exp(lo), xmax = exp(hi)), height = 0, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_point(aes(x = exp(yi), size = weight), shape = 15, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_polygon(data = diamond, aes(x, y), fill = pal[["rust"]]) +
  # left text column: study names
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.012, label = study), hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.012, y = 0, label = "Random effects (REML)", hjust = 0,
           size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.012, y = -0.9, label = "Prediction interval", hjust = 0,
           size = 4.6, colour = pal[["rust"]]) +
  # right text columns: RR [CI] and weight
  geom_text(aes(x = 9, label = label), hjust = 0, size = 4.8) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 45, label = wlab), hjust = 0, size = 4.8, colour = pal[["grey"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 9, y = 0, label = pool_lab, hjust = 0, size = 4.8, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = c(9, 45), y = max(forest_df$row) + 1.2,
           label = c("RR [95% CI]", "Weight"), hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = c(0.25, 4), y = -2, label = c("← Favours vaccine", "Favours control →"),
           size = 4.8, colour = pal[["grey"]]) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4), labels = c("0.1", "0.25", "0.5", "1", "2", "4")) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 6), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.012, 90), ylim = c(-2.2, max(forest_df$row) + 1.4), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))
```

## Anatomy of a forest plot

- **Square** = point estimate of each study; **size** ∝ weight
- **Horizontal line** = 95% CI of that study
- **Vertical line at 1** (ratio) or 0 (difference) = line of no effect
- **Diamond** = pooled estimate; **width** = its 95% CI
- **Prediction interval** = expected range of true effects in a new setting
- Look for: direction, overlap of CIs, outliers, and the heterogeneity statistics

::: {.keybox}
Ask: *Do most studies point the same way? Is the diamond clear of the null? How wide is the spread?*
:::

# Explaining heterogeneity {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## Subgroup analysis

```{r}
#| label: figx-subgroup
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
sub <- bcg_es |>
  mutate(alloc = str_to_title(alloc)) |>
  nest(.by = alloc) |>
  mutate(
    fit  = map(data, \(d) rma(yi, vi, data = d)),
    k    = map_int(fit, \(f) f$k),
    est  = map_dbl(fit, \(f) f$b[1]),
    lo   = map_dbl(fit, \(f) f$ci.lb),
    hi   = map_dbl(fit, \(f) f$ci.ub),
    i2   = map_dbl(fit, \(f) f$I2)
  )

sub_test <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ alloc, data = bcg_es)

sub |>
  ggplot(aes(exp(est), fct_rev(alloc))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = pal[["grey"]]) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = exp(lo), xmax = exp(hi)), height = 0.15,
                 colour = pal[["navy"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(shape = 18, size = 7, colour = pal[["rust"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = str_glue("k = {k}, I² = {fmt(i2, 0)}%")),
            nudge_y = 0.3, colour = pal[["grey"]], size = 4.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Pooled risk ratio (log scale)", y = "Method of allocation",
       title = "Does the effect differ by how participants were allocated?",
       subtitle = str_glue("Test for subgroup differences: p = {fmt(sub_test$QMp, 2)}"))
```

::: {.small}
Pre-specify subgroups, keep them few, and compare them with a **formal interaction test**, not by eyeballing p-values.
:::

## Meta-regression: effect vs latitude

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| label: figx-metareg
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
mr <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = bcg_es)

line_df <- tibble(ablat = seq(10, 56, by = 1)) |>
  mutate(fit = map(ablat, \(x) predict(mr, newmods = x) |> as_tibble())) |>
  unnest(fit)

bcg_es |>
  ggplot(aes(ablat, exp(yi))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = pal[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(data = line_df, aes(x = ablat, ymin = exp(ci.lb), ymax = exp(ci.ub)),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = pal[["rust"]], alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = line_df, aes(ablat, exp(pred)), colour = pal[["rust"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(size = 1 / vi), shape = 21, fill = pal[["teal"]], colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 12), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Absolute latitude of trial site (degrees)", y = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
- Bubble size = study precision
- Further from the equator, **more** protection
- Latitude explains **`r fmt(mr$R2, 0)`%** of the between-study variance (*R*²)
- Needs ~10 studies per covariate
- Observational: **study-level** associations can mislead (ecological bias)
:::
::::

## Sensitivity analysis: leave one out

```{r}
#| label: figx-loo
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
loo <- leave1out(re) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(omitted = bcg_es$study) |>
  mutate(omitted = fct_reorder(omitted, estimate))

loo |>
  ggplot(aes(exp(estimate), omitted)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = exp(re$ci.lb), xmax = exp(re$ci.ub), ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = pal[["rust"]], alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(re$b[1]), colour = pal[["rust"]]) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = exp(ci.lb), xmax = exp(ci.ub)), height = 0, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["navy"]], size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Pooled RR when this study is omitted", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Shaded band: 95% CI of the full analysis. No single trial drives the result.")
```

::: {.small}
Also re-run excluding high risk-of-bias studies, using a different model, or a different effect measure.
:::

# Small-study effects {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## The funnel plot

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r}
#| label: figx-funnel
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 5.2
se_max <- max(bcg_es$sei) * 1.1
funnel_lines <- tibble(se = seq(0, se_max, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(lo = re$b[1] - 1.96 * se, hi = re$b[1] + 1.96 * se)

bcg_es |>
  ggplot(aes(yi, sei)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = bind_rows(
      funnel_lines |> transmute(x = lo, y = se),
      funnel_lines |> arrange(desc(se)) |> transmute(x = hi, y = se)
    ),
    aes(x, y), fill = pal[["soft"]], colour = pal[["grey"]], linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = re$b[1], colour = pal[["rust"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, colour = pal[["navy"]]) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "log risk ratio", y = "Standard error",
       subtitle = "Dot = trial; shaded = 95% pseudo-CI region")
```
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Large studies sit at the **top**, near the pooled effect
- Small studies scatter more widely at the **bottom**
- **Asymmetry** (a missing corner) suggests small-study effects, e.g. publication bias
- But asymmetry also arises from heterogeneity, chance or poor quality
- Need **≥ 10 studies** to interpret
:::
::::

## Testing and adjusting for asymmetry

```{r}
#| label: pubbias
egger <- regtest(re)
tf <- trimfill(re)
```

| Method | What it does | BCG result |
|---|---|---|
| **Egger's test** | Regresses effect on its SE; slope ≠ 0 signals asymmetry | p = `r fmt(egger$pval, 2)` |
| Begg's test | Rank correlation version | Lower power |
| **Trim-and-fill** | Imputes "missing" studies to make the funnel symmetric | `r tf$k0` study added; RR `r fmt(exp(coef(re)))` → `r fmt(exp(coef(tf)))` |

::: {.keybox}
These are **sensitivity analyses**, not corrections. Searching trial registries and grey literature does more to prevent publication bias than any test.
:::

# Certainty of evidence: GRADE {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## From pooled estimate to recommendation

RCTs start at **High**, observational studies at **Low**; final rating: **High · Moderate · Low · Very low**.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Rate down** for

1. **Risk of bias**
2. **Inconsistency** (heterogeneity, *I*²)
3. **Indirectness** (PICO mismatch)
4. **Imprecision** (wide CI, few events)
5. **Publication bias**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Rate up** (mainly observational) for

1. **Large magnitude** of effect
2. **Dose–response** gradient
3. **Plausible confounding** would reduce the effect
:::
::::

::: {.keybox .small}
Present the ratings, outcome by outcome, in a *Summary of Findings* table (GRADEpro).
:::

## Where meta-analysis meets GRADE

```{r}
#| label: tblx-grade
tribble(
  ~Domain,          ~`What the meta-analysis shows you`,                 ~BCG,
  "Risk of bias",   "RoB judgements; sensitivity analysis by RoB",       "Some trials used alternation",
  "Inconsistency",  "Forest plot overlap, I², τ², prediction interval", str_glue("I² = {fmt(re$I2, 0)}%: partly explained by latitude"),
  "Indirectness",   "Do the studies match your PICO?",                   "Mixed populations and decades",
  "Imprecision",    "Width of the pooled CI vs decision thresholds",     str_glue("CI {fmt(exp(re$ci.lb))} to {fmt(exp(re$ci.ub))}"),
  "Publication bias","Funnel plot, Egger, trim-and-fill",                "No strong signal"
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.small .muted}
Illustrative only. A real GRADE assessment is done per outcome by the review team.
:::

# Doing it in R {background-color="#12355B" .divider}

## A complete meta-analysis in a few lines

```{r}
#| label: code-full
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(metafor)

res <- dat.bcg |>
  escalc(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
         data = _, slab = paste0(author, " (", year, ")")) |>
  rma(yi, vi, data = _, method = "REML", test = "knha")   # random effects + HKSJ

res                                 # pooled estimate, tau^2, I^2, Q
predict(res, transf = exp)          # RR with CI and prediction interval
forest(res, atransf = exp)          # forest plot
funnel(res); regtest(res)           # funnel plot and Egger's test
rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = res$data)   # meta-regression
leave1out(res, transf = exp)        # sensitivity analysis
```

::: {.small}
The **meta** package (`metabin()`, `metacont()`, `metagen()`) gives Cochrane-style output with the same ideas. See Schwarzer, Carpenter & Rücker, *Meta-Analysis with R* (Springer, 2015).
:::

## Software options

| Tool | Strengths |
|---|---|
| **R: metafor, meta** | Free, reproducible, every method in this talk and more |
| RevMan (Cochrane) | Standard for Cochrane reviews; GRADEpro integration |
| Stata (`meta`) | Good built-in suite |
| JASP / jamovi | Point-and-click front ends to metafor |
| GRADEpro GDT | Summary of Findings tables and evidence profiles |

## Common pitfalls

- Pooling studies that answer **different questions**
- Choosing fixed vs random **after** seeing *I*²
- Treating *I*² as an absolute measure of heterogeneity (it depends on study precision)
- Double-counting arms of multi-arm trials
- Mixing change scores and final values with the SMD
- Data-dredging through many unplanned subgroups
- Ignoring risk of bias in the synthesis
- Reporting a pooled estimate without a **prediction interval**

## Take-home messages

::: {.bigq}
A meta-analysis is only as good as the systematic review behind it.
:::

1. Ask whether pooling makes sense **before** you pool
2. Inverse-variance weighting: precise studies count for more
3. Random effects estimates an **average**; report τ² and the prediction interval
4. Heterogeneity is information: try to **explain** it
5. Funnel plots and Egger's test are sensitivity checks, not proof
6. Finish with **GRADE**: how sure are we?
